title: AI Workflows with Gumloop
description: Build AI-first automations with Gumloop: flows, AI nodes, web scraping, subflows, and three complete real-world automations you can build today.

lessons.title: The AI-First Automation Platform
lessons.bodyMd:
## The AI first automation platform

Gumloop is a visual automation platform built from the ground up around AI. Where older tools started with "connect app A to app B" and added AI later, Gumloop started with the question: what if AI models were first class citizens in every workflow?

You build **flows** on a drag and drop canvas by connecting **nodes**. Each node does one job: scrape a webpage, ask an AI model a question, send an email, read a spreadsheet. Connect them and you have an automation that can read, reason, and act.

## Who built it and why it matters

Gumloop was founded in 2023 by Max Brodeur-Urbas (ex Microsoft) and Rahul Behal (ex AWS), two engineers who met at McGill University. They saw that AI models were powerful but trapped inside chat windows, and that getting AI into real business workflows required engineering teams most companies do not have.

Their bet: give non engineers a canvas where AI nodes sit next to regular app nodes, and suddenly marketers, recruiters, and founders can build AI workflows that used to require developers.

## What makes it different

Three design choices define Gumloop:

**AI nodes are native, not bolted on.** Asking an AI model to summarize, classify, extract, or rewrite is as easy as adding any other node. You do not need your own API keys for the models; the platform handles model access and folds it into its credit system.

**The web scraper is a star.** Gumloop's scraper node can pull structured data from websites with AI assisted extraction. For lead research, competitive monitoring, and content gathering, this single node replaces a whole category of scraping tools.

**Interfaces for non builders.** You can wrap a flow in a simple form based interface, so teammates use your automation by filling in a form, without ever seeing the canvas. This turns your flows into internal tools.

## The honest caveat

Gumloop has a steeper learning curve than its marketing suggests, and its credit based pricing rewards careful design. It also has fewer native app connectors than older platforms. Go in knowing that, and it is a genuinely powerful tool for AI heavy automation.

## The credit model in plain English

Gumloop runs on credits. Every node execution costs credits, and AI heavy nodes cost more because they burn model compute. The free plan includes a monthly credit allowance, which is plenty for learning and for running small real flows. Paid tiers add more credits.

This model has a nice property: your AI usage is bundled into one bill. You do not need separate API keys or separate subscriptions for the models; the platform handles it. The tradeoff is that you should design with cost in mind. A flow that scrapes fifty pages and runs three AI calls per page, every hour, will eat credits fast. Prototype on a small sample, check the per run cost, then scale deliberately.

## Where Gumloop fits in your toolkit

Gumloop does not replace everything. It is the AI first specialist in a stack that might also include Make or n8n for pure app plumbing. A sensible division: use Make or Zapier for moving data between apps on triggers, and use Gumloop where the workflow needs reading, reasoning, or generating. Many builders use both, each for what it does best.

lessons.title: Why AI-First Changes What You Automate
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why AI first changes what you automate

Traditional automation moves data: new row here becomes a message there. Useful, but limited to work that follows exact rules. AI first automation handles work that needs judgment: reading a messy email and deciding what it means, researching a company from its website, turning a rambling transcript into structured notes.

## The work only AI can automate

Think about the tasks you avoid automating because they need a human brain:

- Reading inbound leads and deciding which are worth pursuing.
- Summarizing long documents into the three points that matter.
- Researching a prospect's company before a call.
- Turning a video into a blog post.
- Reviewing resumes against a job description.

Each of these is pattern recognition plus judgment, which is exactly what AI models do well. Gumloop's whole design is about chaining these judgment steps together with regular app actions: research with AI, then write the result to your CRM; summarize with AI, then post it to Slack.

## How this differs from chatting with AI

You already use AI chat for one off tasks. Gumloop turns those one offs into systems. The difference is triggers and repetition: instead of pasting each new lead into a chat window, a flow watches for new leads and processes each one the same way, every time, without you touching it.

## The mental model: flows as employees

A useful way to think about Gumloop flows is as tireless junior employees. You would not ask a junior employee to "handle marketing." You would give them a specific repeatable process: "every morning, check these three sites, summarize what changed, and post it in this channel." Flows work the same way. Specific process, clear inputs, defined outputs. The AI nodes provide the judgment; the canvas provides the process.

## What you will build in this guide

You will build your first flow, learn the essential nodes, and then build three complete real world automations: a lead research machine, a content repurposing engine, and a daily intelligence digest. By the end you will think in flows, which is the skill that transfers everywhere.

## From tasks to outcomes

Traditional automation thinks in tasks: move this file, send that notification. AI first automation thinks in outcomes: "every lead gets researched before the call," "every piece of content reaches every channel," "I start each day knowing what changed." The flow is the mechanism, but the outcome is the product. When you pitch a flow to your team or a client, sell the outcome, not the nodes.

## The judgment sandwich

The most reliable AI flows follow a pattern: deterministic input, AI judgment in the middle, deterministic output. A spreadsheet provides the lead list (deterministic), AI researches and scores each lead (judgment), and the results land back in the spreadsheet (deterministic). The AI never touches the raw inputs or the final storage directly. This sandwich keeps the unpredictable part contained where you can inspect it, which is why these flows stay trustworthy at scale.

## What still needs humans

AI first does not mean human free. The flows in this guide keep humans on approval, review, and send buttons for anything external. Automation handles the 90 percent that is repetitive; humans handle the 10 percent that needs taste, accountability, or a relationship. Teams that respect this boundary get the leverage without the embarrassing mistakes.

lessons.title: The Vocabulary: Flows, Nodes, and Credits
lessons.bodyMd:
## The five terms that matter

**Flow.** One complete automation in Gumloop, equivalent to a scenario in Make or a Zap in Zapier. A flow has a start, a series of nodes, and an end. You build it on the canvas, test it, then let it run on a schedule or trigger.

**Node.** A single step in a flow. Nodes are the building blocks: the Web Scraper node, the Ask AI node, the Gmail node, the Google Sheets node. Each node takes inputs from connected nodes, does its job, and passes outputs onward.

**Canvas.** The visual workspace where you drag nodes and draw connections between them. Data flows along the connections from left to right. The canvas is also where you test: run the flow and watch data move through each node.

**Credits.** Gumloop's billing unit. Running nodes costs credits, and AI heavy nodes cost more than simple ones because they consume model compute. The free plan includes a monthly credit allowance so you can learn and run real flows. Heavier usage moves you to paid tiers. Design with credits in mind: a flow that scrapes and summarizes fifty pages daily will cost real money, so prototype small.

**Interface.** A simplified front end for a flow: a form where someone types inputs and gets outputs, without seeing the canvas. Interfaces turn your flows into shareable internal tools. Build the lead researcher once, give the sales team an interface, and they use it without learning Gumloop.

## Inputs and outputs

Every node declares what it needs (inputs) and what it produces (outputs). When you connect two nodes, you map the previous node's outputs into the next node's inputs, the same mapping concept you learned in the Make guide. The Ask AI node, for example, takes a prompt as input and produces the model's response as output.

## Triggers and schedules

Flows can run manually (click run), on a schedule (every morning at 8), or via events like webhooks. Scheduled runs are how flows become systems instead of demos. Start every flow with manual runs while testing, then add the schedule once the outputs are trustworthy.

## Node categories you will meet

Nodes group into families. **AI nodes** ask models to summarize, classify, extract, or generate. **Web nodes** scrape pages and interact with sites. **App nodes** connect to tools like Gmail, Sheets, Slack, and Notion. **Logic nodes** filter, branch, and loop. **Input and output nodes** define how data enters and leaves the flow. You do not need to memorize the catalog; you need to recognize which family solves your current problem.

## Mapping: the core skill

Connecting nodes is easy; mapping data between them is the real skill. When the Ask AI node needs the scraped text, you open its settings and map the scraper's output field into the prompt. Good mapping means the right data reaches the right node in the right shape. Most flow bugs are mapping bugs: the wrong field, an empty field, or text where a list was expected. Inspect node inputs during test runs until mapping feels natural.

## Thinking in runs

Every flow execution is a **run**: one pass through the canvas with one set of inputs. Runs can succeed, fail, or partially complete. The run history is your flight recorder: it shows what happened, what each node received and produced, and where things broke. Professionals check run history the way pilots check instruments, routinely, not just when something crashes.

lessons.title: Canvas Tour and Your First AI Node
lessons.bodyMd:
## Setting up

Create an account at gumloop.com. The free plan gives you monthly credits, enough to build everything in this guide. Take the tour if offered, then open a blank flow to see the canvas: an empty workspace with a node palette on the side.

## The canvas tour

**Node palette.** Usually on the left or accessible via a plus button. Nodes are grouped by category: AI, web, Google Workspace, communication, and more. You can also search by name. There are also templates: pre built flows for common jobs, which are excellent learning material.

**The canvas.** The open area where flows live. Drag a node in, drop it, then drag from its output handle to the next node's input handle to connect them. Pan by dragging the background, zoom with the scroll wheel.

**Node configuration.** Click any node to open its settings panel. This is where you write prompts, pick models, enter URLs, and map inputs from previous nodes. The settings panel is where flows are really built; the canvas just shows the structure.

**Run and inspect.** The run button executes the flow. After a run, click nodes to see what data passed through them, just like inspecting bundles in Make. When a node fails, its error message appears here.

## Your first node: Ask AI

Drag an **Ask AI** node onto the canvas. Click it and write a prompt: "Write a three bullet summary of why automation matters for small businesses." Pick a model if the node offers a choice. Click run. The node returns the model's answer as its output.

Congratulations: you just ran an AI model inside a workflow. No API keys, no code, no chat window.

## Making it a flow

One node is a demo; a flow connects nodes. Add a second node after Ask AI: a **Google Docs** or **Notion** node that saves text. Map the Ask AI output into the document content field. Run the flow. Your AI generated summary now lands in a document automatically.

You have learned the core loop of Gumloop: node, configure, connect, map, run, inspect. Every flow in this guide is that loop repeated with more interesting nodes.

## Working with templates

Before building from scratch, open the template gallery and find a flow close to something you want. Templates serve two purposes: you can run them directly for quick value, and you can open them to study their structure. Reading a well built template teaches you which nodes experienced builders choose, how they write prompts, and how they organize the canvas. Treat templates as textbooks, not just shortcuts.

## Keyboard and canvas habits

Learn the canvas shortcuts early: duplicating nodes, aligning them, zooming to fit. Keep canvases tidy from the start: arrange nodes left to right in execution order, keep related nodes grouped, and rename nodes to describe their job ("Summarize article" beats "Ask AI 3"). A tidy canvas is a debuggable canvas. Future you, troubleshooting at midnight, will be grateful.

## Your second node pair

After the Ask AI plus document pair, try Ask AI plus email: generate a draft and email it to yourself. Then try scraper plus Ask AI: scrape a page and summarize it. These tiny two node flows build the muscle memory of configure, connect, map, run, inspect. Five tiny flows teach more than one ambitious flow that never quite works.

lessons.title: Building a Research Brief Flow
lessons.bodyMd:
## A flow with a purpose

Let us build something genuinely useful: a flow that takes a topic, researches it with AI, and produces a structured brief. This exercises the full loop: input, AI reasoning, and output.

## Step 1: Define the input

Every useful flow starts with an input. Drag an input node (often called **Input** or **Text Input**) onto the canvas. This is where the topic goes, like "AI automation for dental clinics." When you run the flow manually, you will type the topic here. Later, a schedule or interface can supply it.

## Step 2: Add the research step

Add an **Ask AI** or research oriented node after the input. Write a structured prompt that maps the input:

"Research the business topic below and produce a brief with exactly these sections: 1) What it is (2 sentences), 2) Who it helps most, 3) Three concrete first steps, 4) One common mistake to avoid. Topic: [input]"

The [input] is your mapped field from the input node. Notice the prompt demands a fixed structure. Structured prompts produce structured outputs, which the next nodes can use reliably.

## Step 3: Add the output

Add a **Google Sheets** node (or Docs, or email) after the AI node. Map the AI output into the destination. Run the flow, type a topic, and watch: topic in, structured brief out, saved automatically.

## Step 4: Refine by inspecting

Your first run's output will be imperfect. Maybe the sections are inconsistent, or the brief is too long. This is normal. Open the AI node's settings and tighten the prompt: add length limits ("each section under 60 words"), add an example of the format you want, specify the audience ("write for a non technical business owner"). Run again. Prompt iteration inside flows works exactly like prompt iteration in chat, except the result is a reusable system.

## The habit to build

Every flow follows this rhythm: build small, run, inspect the outputs, tighten, run again. Resist building a ten node flow before your first run. Two nodes working beats ten nodes imagined.

## Making prompts reusable

The research brief prompt you wrote is already a reusable asset. Save the exact wording somewhere, because you will adapt it for other flows: swap "business topic" for "competitor" and you have a competitor brief; swap it for "job candidate" and you have a screening brief. Prompt patterns compound. Builders who keep a small library of proven prompts move dramatically faster than those who rewrite from scratch each time.

## Adding a quality gate

A simple upgrade: add a second Ask AI node after the first that reviews the brief against a checklist. Prompt: "Review the brief below. Does it have all four sections? Is each section under 60 words? Reply with PASS or list the problems. Brief: [brief]". If it fails, the flow can retry or flag it for you. This evaluator pattern catches the sloppy outputs before they reach anyone, and it costs a fraction of a credit per run.

## From one topic to many

Once the single topic flow works, feed it a list: an iterator over spreadsheet rows, each row becoming one run's input, with results written back per row. You have just turned a single shot tool into a batch processor. This is the standard graduation path: manual input, then list input, then schedule.

lessons.title: From Demo to Reliable Automation
lessons.bodyMd:
## Running reliably

A flow that works once manually is a demo. A flow that works every morning at 8 AM unattended is an automation. This lesson covers the gap between the two.

## Schedules

Add a schedule trigger to run your flow automatically: daily, hourly, or on specific days. Start with daily while you build trust. Each scheduled run consumes credits, so a flow that runs hourly costs roughly 24 times a daily one. Match the schedule to how fresh the data needs to be.

## Debugging failed runs

When a run fails, open the run history and click the failed node. Gumloop shows the inputs the node received and the error it produced. The most common failures:

- **Empty input:** An upstream node produced nothing, so the AI node got a blank prompt. Check the upstream node's outputs on that run.
- **Format mismatch:** The AI returned prose where the next node expected a list. Tighten the prompt to demand the exact format.
- **Credit exhaustion:** The run stopped because the monthly credits ran out. Check usage and either upgrade or slim the flow down.
- **External service errors:** The website blocked the scraper, or the email service rejected the send. These are environmental, not logic errors. Add retries or fallback handling.

## Versioning and iteration

Flows evolve. Before a big change, duplicate the flow so you have a working copy to fall back to. Name versions clearly: "Lead researcher v3, with scoring." This five second habit saves hours when an edit breaks something subtle.

## Monitoring

For flows that matter, add a notification node at the end of the failure path, or check run history on a rhythm: daily for critical flows, weekly for the rest. An automation nobody monitors is a liability with a delay. The goal is boring reliability: it runs, it works, you barely think about it.

## From manual to automatic

The graduation checklist before you schedule any flow: it has run successfully five times manually with varied inputs, the outputs are consistently well formatted, failures produce a notification instead of silence, and you know roughly how many credits each run costs. Then set the schedule and let it work.

## The failure notification

Every scheduled flow needs a way to tell you it broke. The simplest version: a final node on the error path that sends you an email or Slack message with the run details. Slightly better: a daily summary flow that checks the run history of your important flows and reports any failures. Silence is the enemy. A flow that fails quietly for two weeks is worse than no flow, because you made decisions assuming it was working.

## Input validation

Most flow failures start with bad input: an empty spreadsheet row, a malformed URL, a topic field someone left blank. Add a filter or check node near the start that validates inputs before the expensive AI nodes run. "If the URL field is empty, stop and log it" saves credits and prevents confusing downstream errors. Validate early, fail loudly, spend credits only on good inputs.

## Documenting your flows

For any flow someone else might touch, add a description: what it does, what it costs per run, who to contact when it breaks. Thirty seconds of documentation per flow prevents hours of archaeology later. If you build flows for clients, this documentation is part of the deliverable, not a nice extra.

lessons.title: Ask AI and Model Strategy
lessons.bodyMd:
## The heart of the platform

AI nodes are why Gumloop exists. They embed model capabilities directly in your flows, and understanding the main ones unlocks most of what the platform can do.

## Ask AI

The workhorse. You write a prompt, optionally map data into it, and get the model's response. Use it for summarizing, classifying, drafting, extracting, rewriting, and brainstorming. Almost every flow in this guide uses at least one Ask AI node.

Prompt discipline matters more here than in chat, because no human is watching. Demand structured output: "Reply with exactly one of: hot, warm, cold." Give one example of input and desired output. Specify length limits. The stricter the prompt, the more reliable the downstream nodes.

## Model choice

When the node lets you pick a model, match the model to the job. Classification, extraction, and formatting are cheap tasks: use a smaller, faster model. Nuanced reasoning, like judging lead quality from a messy website, deserves a stronger model. Using the biggest model for everything is like hiring a senior architect to hang picture frames: it works, but the credit bill will notice.

## Chaining AI nodes

One AI node does one judgment. Chains of AI nodes do sophisticated work. A common chain: node one extracts key facts from a webpage, node two evaluates those facts against your criteria, node three drafts outreach based on the evaluation. Each node has a narrow job with a strict prompt, so errors stay small and debuggable. If the final draft is bad, you can inspect which step went wrong instead of guessing.

## AI plus tools pattern

The most powerful flows pair AI judgment with deterministic tools. AI decides, tools execute: the AI classifies a lead as hot, a Sheets node logs it, a Gmail node sends the follow up. Keep the AI on judgment and the tools on action. AI is unreliable at exact formatting and perfect recall; tools are unreliable at judgment. Each covers the other's weakness.

## A note on consistency

AI outputs vary slightly run to run. For most automation purposes this is fine. Where exact consistency matters, like extracting a price into a spreadsheet, prefer structured extraction prompts ("return only the number, no currency symbol, no text") and validate with a filter or check downstream. Design for 95 percent reliability and a graceful path for the other 5 percent.

## Temperature and determinism

Some AI nodes expose a temperature or creativity setting. Lower values make outputs more consistent and factual; higher values make them more varied and creative. For automation, default to low: you want the classifier to return "hot" every time, not "hot," "warm-ish," and "spicy" across runs. Save high temperature for brainstorming and drafting nodes where variety is the point.

## Few shot examples in flows

The single highest leverage prompt technique for automation is the worked example: show the model one input and the exact output you want, inside the prompt. "Input: 'The app crashed twice today.' Output: complaint." One example often fixes formatting drift that paragraphs of instruction cannot. For extraction tasks, two or three examples covering edge cases make outputs remarkably consistent.

## Caching and repetition

If your flow asks the same question repeatedly, like classifying the same lead twice, consider whether the answer can be stored and reused. A simple lookup: check your results spreadsheet first, and only run the AI node for new items. This pattern, sometimes called memoization, can cut AI credit costs dramatically on recurring flows. The cheapest AI call is the one you do not make.

lessons.title: Web Scraping and the Scrape-Then-Reason Pattern
lessons.bodyMd:
## The web is your database

Gumloop's web scraper node turns any public webpage into structured data inside your flow. Give it a URL and describe what to extract, and AI assisted extraction pulls it out: product names and prices, article headlines, job listings, company details.

## How to use it well

**Be specific about what you want.** "Extract the product name, price, and rating from this page" beats "get the page data." The node performs dramatically better with a clear extraction target.

**One page type at a time.** A flow that scrapes product pages works reliably. A flow that scrapes product pages, blog posts, and homepages with one configuration does not. If you need multiple page types, use separate scraper nodes or separate flows.

**Respect the sites you scrape.** Scrape public data at reasonable volumes. Do not hammer a site with thousands of requests per hour, do not try to bypass logins or paywalls, and check a site's terms if you are building something commercial on scraped data. Sustainable scraping keeps your flows running instead of getting your IP blocked.

## Browser and interaction nodes

Beyond simple scraping, Gumloop offers nodes that interact with pages more deeply. These handle JavaScript heavy sites and multi step interactions. They cost more credits, so use the simple scraper first and escalate only when the simple one fails.

## The scrape then reason pattern

The killer combination is scraper plus Ask AI: scrape a company's website, then ask AI to summarize what the company does, identify its likely challenges, and suggest a personalized talking point. Raw scraped text goes in, business intelligence comes out. This two node pattern powers the lead research automation in the next chapter, and it is worth memorizing.

## Handling failures gracefully

Websites change layouts, block bots, or go down. Design scraper flows with a fallback: if the scrape returns nothing, the flow should log the URL for manual review rather than crashing or, worse, sending AI generated guesses to a customer. A filter checking "did we get data?" before the AI step prevents embarrassing hallucinations built on empty input.

## Pagination and lists

Many valuable pages are lists: search results, directories, product listings. Scraping a list page gives you links, and then you loop over those links scraping each detail page. This two level pattern, list then details, is how you turn a directory into a dataset. Watch the credit math: one list page plus fifty detail pages with AI extraction each is a real bill, so sample first and confirm the data is worth it.

## Scheduling scrape flows politely

Run scraping flows at off peak times and at modest frequencies. Daily is plenty for competitor monitoring; hourly scraping of someone's site is how you get blocked and how you burn credits. Add random delays if the platform supports them. Think of it as being a polite guest: take what you need, do not pound on the door.

## Storing snapshots for change detection

A powerful upgrade: store each scrape's key facts in a spreadsheet or database, then compare today's scrape against yesterday's. The AI node then describes only what changed instead of summarizing everything. "Competitor X raised their starter price from 29 to 39 and added a new testimonial" is infinitely more useful than a full daily summary. Change detection turns raw scraping into genuine intelligence.

lessons.title: Subflows, Custom Nodes, and Interfaces
lessons.bodyMd:
## Subflows: build once, reuse everywhere

A **subflow** is a flow inside a flow: a reusable mini workflow you can call from multiple parent flows. Build your "summarize this text" logic once as a subflow, then call it from your lead researcher, your content repurposer, and your digest builder.

Subflows keep your canvases readable and your logic consistent. When you improve the summarizer, every flow that uses it improves. Without subflows, you copy paste the same three nodes into every flow and maintain five divergent versions forever.

Good subflow candidates: text summarization, lead scoring, email drafting, data cleaning, sentiment checks. Anything you do in more than one flow.

## Custom nodes: escape hatches

When the built in nodes cannot do something, Gumloop lets you build **custom nodes**. This is the power user feature: wrap an API call, a data transformation, or a specialized AI prompt into a node you can reuse like any other. The CEO's own demos highlight the custom node builder as a differentiator.

You do not need custom nodes on day one. Reach for them when you catch yourself working around a missing capability for the third time. That repetition is the signal that a custom node would pay off.

## Interfaces: flows as internal tools

An **interface** puts a simple form in front of your flow. Your teammate types a company name into a form, the flow researches it, and they get a brief back. They never see the canvas, the prompts, or the credit math.

Interfaces are how one builder's work multiplies across a team. Build the lead researcher once, share the interface with sales. Build the content repurposer once, share it with marketing. The builder maintains the flow; everyone else just uses the tool.

## Templates: learn from the gallery

Gumloop maintains a template library of pre built flows for common jobs: lead enrichment, content generation, SEO workflows, and more. Templates are useful two ways: use them directly to get value fast, and open them up to study how experienced builders structure flows. Reading a good template teaches node selection, prompt design, and flow architecture faster than any documentation.

## Designing good subflows

A good subflow does one thing with clear inputs and outputs, like a function in programming. "Summarize text to three bullets" takes text in and returns bullets out. Avoid subflows that secretly depend on outside context or produce side effects like sending emails; those create spooky action at a distance when reused. Name subflows by what they return, not how they work: "lead score" beats "AI scoring chain v2."

## When interfaces beat raw flows

Share the interface, not the canvas, whenever the user is not the builder. Sales reps, clients, and teammates should get a clean form: type the input, get the output. Reserve canvas access for people who will maintain the flow. This separation is what turns a personal automation into a team capability, and it is also how freelancers productize flows: the client buys the interface, you keep the canvas.

## The template contribution loop

As you build, you will create flows worth sharing. Gumloop's template ecosystem grows through builders publishing their work. Publishing a polished template, with a clear description and sample inputs, builds your reputation and helps others. It also forces you to clean up your flow, which improves it. Teaching through templates is one of the fastest ways to deepen your own skill.

lessons.title: The Lead Research Machine
lessons.bodyMd:
## The problem

Sales teams waste hours researching prospects: opening websites, guessing at pain points, writing first lines that sound like templates because they are templates. This flow does the research automatically and drafts outreach that sounds human.

## The flow, node by node

**1. Input.** A company name and website URL. This can come from a form interface your team fills in, a new row in a leads spreadsheet, or a scheduled run over a list.

**2. Web scraper.** Fetch the company's homepage and about page. Extract: what the company does, company size signals, recent news or announcements.

**3. Ask AI: research synthesis.** Prompt: "Based on the company information below, write: 1) a two sentence description of what they do, 2) three likely business challenges, 3) one specific observation I could reference to show I did my homework. Information: [scraped text]"

**4. Ask AI: draft outreach.** Prompt: "Write a 120 word cold email to [contact role] at [company]. Open with the observation below, connect it to one of the challenges, and end with a soft call to action. Keep the tone conversational, not salesy. Observation: [observation], Challenge: [challenge]"

**5. Output.** Write the research and the draft to a spreadsheet row, or send it to the rep via email or Slack. The rep reviews and personalizes before sending. Human in the loop on the send button; automation on everything before it.

## Why it works

The personalization is real because the inputs are real: the observation comes from their actual website, not a mail merge tag. Reps go from 20 minutes of research per prospect to 2 minutes of review. Response rates improve because the emails do not read like automation.

## Credit math

This flow uses a scrape plus two AI calls per prospect. That is a meaningful credit cost per run, which is exactly why the human review step matters: you only spend credits on prospects worth pursuing. Run it over a curated list, not a purchased database of ten thousand.

## Enrichment sources beyond the website

The company website is the starting point, not the whole picture. Stronger versions of this flow add more inputs: recent news via a news search scrape, the prospect's LinkedIn activity, funding announcements, job postings that reveal priorities ("hiring five sales reps" signals growth pains). Each source becomes another input to the synthesis prompt. More signal in means sharper personalization out, but each source adds credits, so add them in order of value and measure whether reply rates actually move.

## Scoring before drafting

A refinement worth adding: score the lead before spending credits on a full draft. A quick Ask AI node rates fit from 1 to 10 based on your ideal customer profile. Below threshold, the flow logs the lead and stops. Above threshold, it writes the full research and draft. This gate keeps your credit spend focused on prospects worth the effort and keeps reps reviewing only qualified drafts.

## Team rollout

When rolling this out to a sales team, start with one rep for two weeks. Tune the prompts based on which drafts they actually send versus rewrite. Then share the interface with the team and track a simple metric: drafts reviewed per week and reply rate. The flow earns its keep when reps say they would not go back to manual research. That sentence is the real success metric.

lessons.title: The Content Repurposing Engine
lessons.bodyMd:
## The problem

You publish a blog post, a video, or a podcast episode, and then it sits in one place while your audience lives in five. Manually repurposing content for each channel is tedious, so it does not happen, and most of your content's value goes unrealized.

## The flow, node by node

**1. Input.** The source content: a blog URL, a video transcript, or pasted text.

**2. Web scraper or transcript fetch.** Pull the full content into the flow.

**3. Ask AI: extract core ideas.** Prompt: "Read the content below and list the 5 key ideas, each in one sentence. Then pick the single most surprising or useful idea. Content: [content]"

**4. Ask AI: channel drafts (parallel).** Three AI nodes, each with a channel specific prompt:
- LinkedIn: "Write a LinkedIn post under 200 words based on the key idea below. Start with a hook line, add line breaks for readability, end with a question. Key idea: [idea]"
- Newsletter: "Write a 150 word newsletter section introducing this idea to subscribers, conversational tone. Idea: [idea]"
- Short video script: "Write a 45 second video script about this idea: hook in the first 3 seconds, one example, one takeaway. Idea: [idea]"

**5. Output.** Save all drafts to a document or Notion page for review. You edit, approve, and publish. The flow does the tedious first draft; you do the judgment.

## Why it works

Repurposing is a transformation task with clear rules per channel, which is exactly what AI nodes do well. The parallel structure means all variants generate in one run. And because the source is your own content, the outputs stay on brand without heavy prompt engineering.

## The review habit

Never auto publish AI drafted content under your name. The flow's job is to take you from blank page to editable draft in seconds. Your job is the 10 minutes of editing that makes it sound like you. This division of labor is the whole point: automation handles volume, humans handle voice.

## Building a content bank

Run the repurposer over your archive, not just new posts. That back catalog of twenty blog posts becomes eighty channel drafts in an afternoon. Store everything in one document or database with status columns: draft, edited, scheduled, published. The content bank turns sporadic publishing into a pipeline: you always have edited drafts waiting, so consistency stops depending on motivation.

## Channel specific tuning

Each channel node deserves its own prompt tuning over time. LinkedIn rewards strong hooks and line breaks. Newsletters reward warmth and a clear takeaway. Video scripts reward spoken language, short sentences, and explicit visual cues. Review published performance monthly: which repurposed pieces actually performed? Feed those winners back into the prompts as examples. The flow gets better the longer it runs, because your taste becomes its training data.

## The batching habit

Run repurposing in weekly batches rather than per post. Friday afternoon: drop the week's content into the flow, review all drafts Monday morning, schedule the week. Batching concentrates the review work into one focused session instead of fragmenting it across the week. Systems beat willpower, and batching is the simplest system there is.

lessons.title: The Daily Intelligence Digest
lessons.bodyMd:
## The problem

Information you need is scattered: industry news, competitor updates, key accounts' announcements. Checking it all manually every morning is a 45 minute ritual nobody enjoys. This flow builds you a personal intelligence briefing.

## The flow, node by node

**1. Schedule.** Runs every weekday at 7 AM.

**2. Inputs: your watchlist.** A spreadsheet with the sites, topics, or companies you track. The flow reads the list each run, so updating your interests means editing a spreadsheet, not rebuilding the flow.

**3. Web scraper (looped).** For each watchlist item, fetch the latest content. Depending on the source this might be a homepage, a blog, or a news search page.

**4. Ask AI: relevance filter.** Prompt: "Below are items from [source]. Identify the ones genuinely new or important for someone tracking [your interest]. Ignore press releases and fluff. Return only the items worth knowing, each as a one line summary with why it matters. Items: [scraped content]"

**5. Ask AI: briefing assembly.** Prompt: "Combine the summaries below into a morning briefing: group by topic, lead with the most important item, keep the whole thing under 300 words. Summaries: [summaries]"

**6. Output.** Send the briefing to your email or Slack every morning. On quiet days the flow says so instead of inventing news: add a filter so that if nothing passed the relevance check, it sends "Nothing significant today" rather than padding.

## Why it works

The relevance filter is the secret. Without it you get a longer pile of links, which is what RSS already gives you. With it you get judgment: an AI read everything and told you what matters. That is the upgrade from aggregation to intelligence.

## Start small

Begin with three sources you actually check manually today. Run the flow for a week and compare its briefing against what you would have found yourself. Tune the relevance prompt based on what it gets wrong. Only expand the watchlist once the briefings are consistently useful. A digest you trust for three sources beats one you ignore for thirty.

## Curating the watchlist

The digest is only as good as its sources. Audit the watchlist monthly: which sources produced items you acted on, and which produced noise you skipped? Cut ruthlessly. A watchlist of five sources you read beats twenty you ignore. Add new sources deliberately when your interests shift, like entering a new market or tracking a new competitor. Curation is the ongoing work; the flow just executes it.

## Weekend and quiet day handling

Not every day needs a briefing. Configure the schedule for weekdays only, and make sure the "nothing significant" path is graceful: a one line message, not an apologetic paragraph. Some builders add a weekly rollup instead: a Friday flow that summarizes the week's briefings into trends. Daily for awareness, weekly for pattern spotting. Both from the same watchlist.

## Sharing the digest with a team

A personal digest becomes a team asset when you forward it to a shared channel. Better: give teammates their own watchlist rows in the spreadsheet and generate per person sections. The marginal cost of one more section is tiny, and suddenly the whole team starts the day informed. Shared context compounds: meetings get shorter when everyone read the same briefing.
